g.text: SIMULATED DATA
EMOTIONAL JOURNEY MAP
One task, six moments, nothing above zero
Core job: take today’s doses on time. Valence −5 to +5, plotted from the transcripts. Emotions are the participant’s own words wherever they offered any.
CAPSTONE 02 · JOURNEY
6 stages · 5 participants · 0 stages invented
EMOTIONAL VALENCE
0 · neutral
everything below this line is negative
WAKING
DECIDING
MIDDAY
EVENING
DISRUPTED
NEXT MORNING
READ THIS
No stage on this
map is emotionally
positive except the
last one.
A happy chart would
STAGE 1 OF 6
Waking
Reluctant restart
The hour and the place are the problem,
not the pill. A 4:40 alarm P1 hates,
or a car park at half six.
WHAT THEY SAY
P1: “I’m up at 4:40, that’s the
alarm I hate most”
P4: “I wake up in a car park outside
someone’s house at half six”
SO THE PRODUCT
Never assume a wall-clock “morning”.
Anchor to a cue the person already
has: coffee, the kettle, the van.
Sources: P1, P4
Distress is about the hour, not the medicine.
STAGE 2 OF 6
Deciding to start
Friction, or ease
Zero because it splits. Simple regimens
drop into a habit that already exists.
Complex ones need a slot you can’t find.
WHAT THEY SAY
P2: “Tablet with the first coffee”
P5: “the pill goes in and the coffee
follows”
P1: “the one I can never find in the
morning. That’s a real problem.”
SO THE PRODUCT
Make the rare dose as findable as the daily
one. Do not bury “as needed” among the
routine slots, and do not ask for a label hunt.
Sources: P1, P2, P5
STAGE 3 OF 6
Midday
Nuisance, not fear
A dose that needs food, and no food
until 11 at night. P4 will not touch a
phone while driving. No safe path.
WHAT THEY SAY
P4: “It doesn’t get taken, or it gets
taken at 11 at night when I finally get
something.”
P4: “I don’t touch my phone when I’m
driving, full stop.”
SO THE PRODUCT
Flexible windows, food-optional guidance,
and never an unlock-and-tap while
someone is moving.
SINGLE SOURCE · P4 only. A hypothesis,
not a requirement. Nobody else said this.
STAGE 4 OF 6
Evening dose
Quiet self-doubt
The window has closed by the time they
get home. The dose is for “about half
seven”. P2 gets in at nine.
WHAT THEY SAY
P2: “do I really need this tonight?
And honestly, the answer’s sometimes no”
P2: “the evening one is a coin toss when
I’m late”
SO THE PRODUCT
Plain lateness guidance instead of a binary
reminder. This person is late, not failing,
and the copy has to know the difference.
Sources: P2, echoed by P4’s 11pm dose
P2 says “late out maybe twice a week” — a hedge, kept as one.
STAGE 5 OF 6
Disrupted days
Three emotions
The worst point on the map, and it is not
one thing. (a) The rota changed — P1, P4.
(b) The routine did not travel — P5.
(c) No idea how bad one miss is — P3.
WHAT THEY SAY
P1: “I felt terrible. Like I’d done
something wrong. I deleted it.”
P3: “I had been afraid of my own
medicine for two weeks…”
SO THE PRODUCT
Factual, non-punitive information about the
real consequence of a single missed dose.
A routine that survives the day it goes wrong.
The AI fused (a), (b) and (c) into one −4,
which hid that they have three different fixes.
STAGE 6 OF 6
Next morning
Mild relief
The only positive stage. The day is behind
them, and some want to answer family
honestly without hesitating first.
WHAT THEY SAY
P1: “Tomorrow’s problem is tomorrow’s.”
P4: “be able to say yes without the
hesitation”
P3: “I don’t want a wall of undoned days.”
SO THE PRODUCT
Let each day start visually clean. No backlog
of undoned days, and no tone about the one
that went wrong.
Sources: P1, P3, P4
P3 rules out the alternative outright.
Three least-bad points
The AI called these “the three highest points”. Two of the three are negative.
Next morning +1 — the only positive stage on the map.
Deciding to start 0 — it splits: ease for two, friction for one.
Waking −2 — the hour is the problem, not the medication.
Internally consistent as a ranking, misleading as a headline. A PM reading
“highest points” on a mood chart assumes positive states. Relabelled,
with the absolute values shown next to every name.
The troughs are the roadmap
Every feature priority should trace to a trough. Peaks get nothing added to them.
Evening −3 (P2) → plain lateness guidance, not a binary reminder.
Disrupted days −4 (P1, P3, P4, P5) → factual, non-punitive
information about one missed dose, and a routine that survives the day.
Midday −3 (P4 only) → flexible windows, food-optional guidance.
One source. Do not put a roadmap on a single participant — and do not put a
feature at a peak, where the pill is already taken and the job is to be quiet.
What the AI got wrong here
Four errors on this map alone. All four are in the verification log.
1. Called midday “anxious improvisation”. P4: “It’s mostly a
nuisance, and I’m not dramatic about it… It’s not fear.”
2. Fused three unrelated failures into one −4, hiding three fixes.
3. Ranked −2 as a “high point” on a chart of mostly negative stages.
4. Let a midday stage built on one participant read as a general truth about
five. The stage now carries the single-source warning on its face.

Valence is the participant’s own description, not a number we invented: every emotion on this map is either quoted or named in the participant’s own words. The scale is a design tool, and it is labelled as one.
Simulated corpus: no human was interviewed. Hedged frequencies stay hedged — P2’s “maybe twice a week” is a quote, not a rate, and appears nowhere on this page as a metric.
